name: Nap
description: Nap (short for Napoleon) is a classic English trick-taking game that gained massive popularity in Britain during the 19th and early 20th centuries. It is a quick, high-stakes game where players bid on how many of their five cards they can win in a trick-based battle against everyone else. Known for its escalating bidding tiers named after Napoleonic battles (Wellington, BlÃ¼cher) and its simple yet ruthless scoring system.

history.origins: Napoleon is a classic English pub game first documented in H.E. Heather's October 1875 edition of The Bazaar. It quickly became England's national five-card game, displacing Loo. Early authors described it as 'spirited and interesting', requiring 'considerable judgement and skill'. The expression 'going Nap' (meaning to risk all on one attempt) derives from this game.
timeline: 1875: Earliest rules published by H.E. Heather in The Bazaar
1885: American Hoyle incorrectly claims French origin; more likely European roots with north German Fipsen as a relative
1891: Bids of Wellington, BlÃ¼cher and MisÃ¨re added; variants like Peep Nap, Sir Garnet, and Jam emerge
1982: Andrew Pennycook notes Nap was 'widely played in pubs'
Present: Still played in southern England, Strathclyde (Scotland), and other parts of Britain
history.cultural: A quintessential British pub game played for small stakes with settlement after each hand. The terminology reflects British military history, with bids named after the Duke of Wellington and General BlÃ¼cher who defeated Napoleon at Waterloo.
history.evolution: The game evolved from simple five-card bidding to include advanced bids like Wellington (overcalls Nap) and BlÃ¼cher (overcalls Wellington). Variants emerged including Peep Nap (with floater card), Purchase Nap (buying cards), and six-, seven-, and nine-card versions.

setup.players: 3-8 players; 4-5 is optimal. No permanent partnershipsâ€”high bidder plays against all others.
setup.deck: Standard 52-card pack. Cards rank A-K-Q-J-10-9-8-7-6-5-4-3-2. Often reduced: 3 players use 20 cards (A-K-Q-J-10), 4 players use 28 (A-8), 5 players use 32 (A-7).
setup.dealing: Five cards to each playerâ€”either 3 then 2, or 2 then 3. Cards are shuffled only at start and after successful Nap/Wellington/BlÃ¼cher bids; otherwise just gathered and cut.
setup.equipment: Standard deck, poker chips or counters for stakes.

rules.objective: Win at least the number of tricks bid. The bidder plays against all other players who form a temporary team.
rules.gameplay: 1. High bidder leads first trick; suit of this card becomes trumps. 2. Players must follow suit if possible. 3. Highest trump wins trick; if no trumps, highest card of led suit wins. 4. Winner of trick leads next.
keyRules: Five cards each; high bidder names trumps by leading
One bidding round onlyâ€”pass or overcall
Wellington can only be bid after Nap; BlÃ¼cher only after Wellington
Cards often not shuffled between hands (just cut)

strategy.basic: Be aggressive with bids if you have high trumps (Ace or King) and at least one other card of the same suit. Since you only have 5 cards, a single strong suit can carry the whole hand. If you aren't the bidder, your only goal is to 'break' the bid by taking just one trick.
strategy.intermediate: The 'Overbid' Defense: If you have a solid hand (e.g., King and Queen of a suit) and someone bids 3, consider bidding 4 just to prevent their certain victory. Even if you fail, you prevent them from winning and force them to play defensively next round.
strategy.advanced: Counting the BlÃ¼cher: Only bid Wellington or BlÃ¼cher if you hold the Ace and King of your lead suit. If someone else holds the Ace, they will almost certainly 'break' you on the first trick. Wellington is a psychological tool to scare away weaker 'Nap' bidders.
tips: If you are a defender, always lead through the bidder to try and find their weak suit
In Nap, the Ace is your most important cardâ€”never waste it on a trick where someone else has already played a trump unless you have to
With a balanced hand and no strong suit, consider passing rather than bidding low

scoring.description: Stake-based payment system. Bidder wins stakes from all opponents if successful; pays all opponents if unsuccessful.
scoring.winCondition: Win at least the number of tricks bid.

synthesis.shortDescription: A spirited British trick-taking game where players bid on winning tricks with just five cards. Famous for its Napoleonic bidding tiers and pub-friendly stakes.
